prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The study involved four groups of participants, with group sizes of 22, 10, 15, and 15, in whom itch was triggered using histamine or cowhage.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers applied sinusoidal and half-sine-wave electrical stimulation to both sensitized and control skin areas to measure itch and pain responses.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The method for selectively activating C-fibres was confirmed by blocking A-fibres.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Pre-treating the skin with an itch-inducing agent significantly increased the chance that electrical C-fibre stimulation would be felt as itch at the treated site compared to untreated skin.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The intensity of the electrically induced itch did not increase with stronger stimulation, whereas pain ratings did show a clear dependence on stimulus intensity.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Mapping the skin showed a secondary area of itch sensitivity that was similar in size to areas of mechanical itch sensitivity and larger than the typical receptive fields of primary nerve endings.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Applying local cooling significantly reduced the itch caused by histamine and lowered the likelihood that C-fibre stimulation would be perceived as itchy.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: C-fibre hyperknesis was more common in participants who still had spontaneous itch (61.9%) than in those whose itch had resolved (29.2%).
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results show that spinal itch sensitization includes C-fibre input and is maintained by ongoing itch activity.
facts.subject: humans
